# Unit 1 Calendar Events, Paste-Ready

**Unit 1: The Global Tapestry**, Topics 1.1 to 1.7, one calendar event per topic.

**Generated by `tools/build-canvas-events.js`. Do not hand-edit.**
LEARNING TARGETS and SUCCESS CRITERIA are lifted verbatim from each topic's
data file and renderer-config, run in the order the lesson shell loads them, so
the config wins wherever the two disagree, exactly as it does for a student.
Change a target in the source file and rerun the generator; never edit a target
in Canvas, and never edit it here.

OVERVIEW prose is hand-written in the `UNIT_OVERVIEWS` table inside the
generator. Unit data files carry no `commandCopy`, so each one is written from
that topic's own `lecture.intro`, targets, and criteria, in student-facing
voice. Edit it there, then rerun.

```bash
node tools/build-canvas-events.js          # write
node tools/build-canvas-events.js --check  # fail on drift, write nothing
```

## How to paste one of these

1. Canvas Calendar, click the day, **Edit**, then **More Options**.
2. Title the event exactly as given below.
3. In the Rich Content Editor, click the **`</>`** icon to open the HTML editor.
   **Never paste this into the visual editor.** Pasting rendered HTML there
   injects wrapper `<div>`s and inline font declarations that collapse the table.
4. Paste the whole `<table>` block.
5. Switch back to the visual editor, delete the `[INSERT ASSIGNMENT LINK]`
   placeholder text, and insert the real assignment from the right-hand
   course-links panel, **Assignments**, click the assignment. Do not hand-type
   that link; see Section 5 of `CANVAS-BUILD-GUIDE.md` for why.
6. Save.

Build the seven Canvas assignments before the seven events. The course-links
panel in step 5 can only insert an assignment that already exists; see Section 11
of `CANVAS-BUILD-GUIDE.md` for the full per-topic procedure and Section 7 for the
assignment settings.

All seven links point at the live GitHub Pages build:
`https://jeffandersonlogic.github.io/ap-world-history/unit-1/`

Module hub, for the module's `[External]` item:
`https://jeffandersonlogic.github.io/ap-world-history/unit-1/index.html`

## APW - 1.1 - Song China

**Event title:** `APW - 1.1 - Song China`  
**Assignment to link:** `1.1 - Song China`  
**Source data files:** `assets/data/lesson-1-1-song-china.js`, `assets/data/lesson-1-1-renderer-config.js`  
**Lesson page:** `unit-1/lesson-1-1-song-china.html`

```html
<table style="border-collapse: collapse; width: 100%; border-color: #000000; border-style: solid;" border="3" cellpadding="8">
    <tbody>
        <tr>
            <td style="width: 20%; vertical-align: top; background-color: #f0f0f0;">
                <h3>OVERVIEW</h3>
            </td>
            <td style="vertical-align: top;">
                <p>Song China ran on a system rather than on one strong ruler, and today you take that system apart. You trace how Confucianism, the imperial bureaucracy, and the civil service exam decided who governed and made that rule feel legitimate; how Chinese cultural traditions and Buddhism kept shaping East Asia and its neighbors; and how Champa rice, the Grand Canal, paper money, and expanding trade built one of the most commercialized economies of the postclassical world. The work is connecting each piece of evidence to a specific effect, not listing the pieces.</p>
            </td>
        </tr>
        <tr>
            <td style="width: 20%; vertical-align: top; background-color: #f0f0f0;">
                <h3>LEARNING TARGETS</h3>
            </td>
            <td style="vertical-align: top;">
                <ol>
                    <li>I can explain how Song China used Confucianism, imperial bureaucracy, and civil service exams to maintain and justify rule.</li>
                    <li>I can describe how Chinese cultural traditions and Buddhism continued to shape East Asia and influence neighboring regions.</li>
                    <li>I can explain how agricultural innovation, infrastructure, and commercialization strengthened Song China's economy and connections to wider trade networks.</li>
                </ol>
            </td>
        </tr>
        <tr>
            <td style="width: 20%; vertical-align: top; background-color: #f0f0f0;">
                <h3>SUCCESS CRITERIA</h3>
            </td>
            <td style="vertical-align: top;">
                <ol>
                    <li>I can use specific evidence such as bureaucracy, civil service exams, Confucianism, or Neo-Confucianism to explain how Song rulers organized power.</li>
                    <li>I can explain how Confucianism, Buddhism, and Chinese cultural traditions continued or changed as they shaped societies in East Asia.</li>
                    <li>I can connect Champa rice, the Grand Canal, paper money, trade, and production to population growth, urbanization, and commercial expansion.</li>
                </ol>
            </td>
        </tr>
        <tr>
            <td style="width: 20%; vertical-align: top; background-color: #f0f0f0;">
                <h3>BeHistorical Link</h3>
            </td>
            <td style="vertical-align: top;">

            </td>
        </tr>
        <tr>
```

## APW - 1.2 - Developments in Dar al-Islam

**Event title:** `APW - 1.2 - Developments in Dar al-Islam`  
**Assignment to link:** `1.2 - Dar al-Islam`  
**Source data files:** `assets/data/lesson-1-2-dar-al-islam.js`, `assets/data/lesson-1-2-renderer-config.js`  
**Lesson page:** `unit-1/lesson-1-2-dar-al-islam.html`

```html
<table style="border-collapse: collapse; width: 100%; border-color: #000000; border-style: solid;" border="3" cellpadding="8">
    <tbody>
        <tr>
            <td style="width: 20%; vertical-align: top; background-color: #f0f0f0;">
                <h3>OVERVIEW</h3>
            </td>
            <td style="vertical-align: top;">
                <p>By c. 1200 the Abbasid Caliphate no longer held political control of the Islamic world, and Dar al-Islam kept expanding anyway. Today you work out how both things are true at once: political fragmentation into states such as the Seljuk Empire, the Mamluk Sultanate, and the Delhi Sultanate, alongside continued expansion carried by merchants, missionaries, and Sufi networks rather than only by armies. You also examine what scholars in those states did with translation, paper-making, mathematics, medicine, astronomy, and geography, and why that scholarship traveled as far as it did.</p>
            </td>
        </tr>
        <tr>
            <td style="width: 20%; vertical-align: top; background-color: #f0f0f0;">
                <h3>LEARNING TARGETS</h3>
            </td>
            <td style="vertical-align: top;">
                <ol>
                    <li>I can explain how systems of belief and their practices affected society in the period from c. 1200 to c. 1450.</li>
                    <li>I can explain the causes and effects of the rise of Islamic states over time.</li>
                    <li>I can explain the effects of intellectual innovation in Dar al-Islam.</li>
                </ol>
            </td>
        </tr>
        <tr>
            <td style="width: 20%; vertical-align: top; background-color: #f0f0f0;">
                <h3>SUCCESS CRITERIA</h3>
            </td>
            <td style="vertical-align: top;">
                <ol>
                    <li>I can describe how Islamic states changed after Abbasid fragmentation and identify examples such as the Seljuk Empire, Mamluk Sultanate, and Delhi Sultanate.</li>
                    <li>I can explain how Islam spread through military expansion, merchants, missionaries, and Sufi networks.</li>
                    <li>I can connect scholarship, translation, paper-making, mathematics, medicine, astronomy, and geography to intellectual exchange.</li>
                </ol>
            </td>
        </tr>
        <tr>
            <td style="width: 20%; vertical-align: top; background-color: #f0f0f0;">
                <h3>BeHistorical Link</h3>
            </td>
            <td style="vertical-align: top;">
                <p><a class="inline_disabled" href="https://jeffandersonlogic.github.io/ap-world-history/unit-1/lesson-1-2-dar-al-islam.html" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Topic 1.2 - Developments in Dar al-Islam</a></p>
            </td>
        </tr>
        <tr>
            <td style="width: 20%; vertical-align: top; background-color: #f0f0f0;">
```

## APW - 1.3 - Developments in South and Southeast Asia

**Event title:** `APW - 1.3 - Developments in South and Southeast Asia`  
**Assignment to link:** `1.3 - South and SE Asia`  
**Source data files:** `assets/data/lesson-1-3-south-southeast-asia.js`, `assets/data/lesson-1-3-renderer-config.js`  
**Lesson page:** `unit-1/lesson-1-3-south-southeast-asia.html`

```html
<table style="border-collapse: collapse; width: 100%; border-color: #000000; border-style: solid;" border="3" cellpadding="8">
    <tbody>
        <tr>
            <td style="width: 20%; vertical-align: top; background-color: #f0f0f0;">
                <h3>OVERVIEW</h3>
            </td>
            <td style="vertical-align: top;">
                <p>South and Southeast Asia is where you watch belief systems work as political tools. Hinduism, Buddhism, and Islam each shaped the societies here, and the states used them: Vijayanagara and the Khmer Empire built power on land, while Srivijaya and Majapahit built it on straits and ports. Today you compare a land-based route to power with a maritime one, and connect trade routes, ports, monsoon winds, and merchant communities to the political and cultural change that followed.</p>
            </td>
        </tr>
        <tr>
            <td style="width: 20%; vertical-align: top; background-color: #f0f0f0;">
                <h3>LEARNING TARGETS</h3>
            </td>
            <td style="vertical-align: top;">
                <ol>
                    <li>I can explain how Hinduism, Buddhism, and Islam shaped societies and states in South and Southeast Asia.</li>
                    <li>I can describe how states such as the Vijayanagara Empire, Delhi Sultanate, Srivijaya, Majapahit, and Khmer Empire used religion, trade, and administration to build power.</li>
                    <li>I can explain how Indian Ocean trade connected South and Southeast Asia to wider Afro-Eurasian networks.</li>
                </ol>
            </td>
        </tr>
        <tr>
            <td style="width: 20%; vertical-align: top; background-color: #f0f0f0;">
                <h3>SUCCESS CRITERIA</h3>
            </td>
            <td style="vertical-align: top;">
                <ol>
                    <li>I can use specific evidence about Hinduism, Buddhism, Islam, temples, rulers, and merchants to explain how belief systems shaped society.</li>
                    <li>I can compare how land-based states (Vijayanagara, Khmer) and maritime states (Srivijaya, Majapahit) used religion and geography to build power.</li>
                    <li>I can connect trade routes, ports, monsoon winds, and merchant communities to political and cultural change in South and Southeast Asia.</li>
                </ol>
            </td>
        </tr>
        <tr>
            <td style="width: 20%; vertical-align: top; background-color: #f0f0f0;">
                <h3>BeHistorical Link</h3>
            </td>
            <td style="vertical-align: top;">
                <p><a class="inline_disabled" href="https://jeffandersonlogic.github.io/ap-world-history/unit-1/lesson-1-3-south-southeast-asia.html" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Topic 1.3 - Developments in South and Southeast Asia</a></p>
            </td>
        </tr>
        <tr>
```

## APW - 1.4 - State Building in the Americas

**Event title:** `APW - 1.4 - State Building in the Americas`  
**Assignment to link:** `1.4 - States in the Americas`  
**Source data files:** `assets/data/lesson-1-4-americas.js`, `assets/data/lesson-1-4-renderer-config.js`  
**Lesson page:** `unit-1/lesson-1-4-americas.html`

```html
<table style="border-collapse: collapse; width: 100%; border-color: #000000; border-style: solid;" border="3" cellpadding="8">
    <tbody>
        <tr>
            <td style="width: 20%; vertical-align: top; background-color: #f0f0f0;">
                <h3>OVERVIEW</h3>
            </td>
            <td style="vertical-align: top;">
                <p>State building in the Americas happened without contact with Afro-Eurasia, which makes it the cleanest test in Unit 1 of what states have in common. Today you examine Maya city-states, the Mexica, the Inca, and the North American societies at Chaco, Mesa Verde, and Cahokia, asking the same questions of each: how power was organized, what stayed continuous, what was genuinely new, and how far the system reached. You also practice naming the evidence a source uses to support its argument, which is a skill the exam tests directly.</p>
            </td>
        </tr>
        <tr>
            <td style="width: 20%; vertical-align: top; background-color: #f0f0f0;">
                <h3>LEARNING TARGETS</h3>
            </td>
            <td style="vertical-align: top;">
                <ol>
                    <li>I can explain how and why states in the Americas developed and changed over time.</li>
                    <li>I can describe how American state systems demonstrated continuity, innovation, diversity, and expanded in scope and reach.</li>
                    <li>I can identify evidence in a source that supports an argument about state building in the Americas.</li>
                </ol>
            </td>
        </tr>
        <tr>
            <td style="width: 20%; vertical-align: top; background-color: #f0f0f0;">
                <h3>SUCCESS CRITERIA</h3>
            </td>
            <td style="vertical-align: top;">
                <ol>
                    <li>I can use evidence about Maya city-states, Mexica, Inca, Chaco, Mesa Verde, or Cahokia to explain state systems in the Americas.</li>
                    <li>I can explain continuity, innovation, diversity, or expansion in American state systems.</li>
                    <li>I can identify evidence used in a source to support an argument about American state building.</li>
                </ol>
            </td>
        </tr>
        <tr>
            <td style="width: 20%; vertical-align: top; background-color: #f0f0f0;">
                <h3>BeHistorical Link</h3>

            <td style="vertical-align: top;">
                <p><a class="inline_disabled" href="https://jeffandersonlogic.github.io/ap-world-history/unit-1/lesson-1-4-americas.html" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Topic 1.4 - State Building in the Americas</a></p>
```

## APW - 1.5 - State Building in Africa

**Event title:** `APW - 1.5 - State Building in Africa`  
**Assignment to link:** `1.5 - States in Africa`  
**Source data files:** `assets/data/lesson-1-5-africa.js`, `assets/data/lesson-1-5-renderer-config.js`  
**Lesson page:** `unit-1/lesson-1-5-africa.html`

```html
<table style="border-collapse: collapse; width: 100%; border-color: #000000; border-style: solid;" border="3" cellpadding="8">
    <tbody>
        <tr>
            <td style="width: 20%; vertical-align: top; background-color: #f0f0f0;">
                <h3>OVERVIEW</h3>
            </td>
            <td style="vertical-align: top;">
                <p>Great Zimbabwe, Ethiopia, and the Hausa city-states each built power out of what their position gave them. Today you connect Great Zimbabwe's stone enclosures and gold to Indian Ocean trade, Ethiopia's Solomonic dynasty and Christianity to control of Red Sea routes, and Hausa Islamic administration to the trans-Saharan network. The move worth practicing is treating religion as a tool of governance and not only as belief: ask what work Christianity or Islam actually did for the ruler using it.</p>
            </td>
        </tr>
        <tr>
            <td style="width: 20%; vertical-align: top; background-color: #f0f0f0;">
                <h3>LEARNING TARGETS</h3>
            </td>
            <td style="vertical-align: top;">
                <ol>
                    <li>I can explain how and why states in Africa developed and changed from c. 1200 to c. 1450.</li>
                    <li>I can describe how trade, religion, and geography shaped state power in Great Zimbabwe, Ethiopia, and the Hausa kingdoms.</li>
                    <li>I can explain how Islam and Christianity functioned as tools of governance, not just belief, in African states.</li>
                </ol>
            </td>
        </tr>
        <tr>
            <td style="width: 20%; vertical-align: top; background-color: #f0f0f0;">
                <h3>SUCCESS CRITERIA</h3>
            </td>
            <td style="vertical-align: top;">
                <ol>
                    <li>I can use specific evidence about Great Zimbabwe's stone enclosures, gold trade, and Indian Ocean connections to explain how it built power.</li>
                    <li>I can explain how Ethiopia's Solomonic dynasty used Christianity and control of Red Sea trade to maintain independence and legitimacy.</li>
                    <li>I can describe how Hausa city-states used trans-Saharan trade and Islamic administration to build and exercise power.</li>
                </ol>
            </td>
        </tr>
        <tr>
            <td style="width: 20%; vertical-align: top; background-color: #f0f0f0;">
                <h3>BeHistorical Link</h3>
            </td>
            <td style="vertical-align: top;">
                <p><a class="inline_disabled" href="https://jeffandersonlogic.github.io/ap-world-history/unit-1/lesson-1-5-africa.html" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Topic 1.5 - State Building in Africa</a></p>
```

## APW - 1.6 - Developments in Europe

**Event title:** `APW - 1.6 - Developments in Europe`  
**Assignment to link:** `1.6 - Developments in Europe`  
**Source data files:** `assets/data/lesson-1-6-europe.js`, `assets/data/lesson-1-6-renderer-config.js`  
**Lesson page:** `unit-1/lesson-1-6-europe.html`

```html
<table style="border-collapse: collapse; width: 100%; border-color: #000000; border-style: solid;" border="3" cellpadding="8">
    <tbody>
        <tr>
            <td style="width: 20%; vertical-align: top; background-color: #f0f0f0;">
                <h3>OVERVIEW</h3>
            </td>
            <td style="vertical-align: top;">
                <p>Europe is the outlier of Unit 1, and that is exactly what makes it useful. Where Song China centralized, Europe fragmented: monarchs shared power with nobles and with the Church, feudalism and manorialism organized land and labor, and towns, guilds, and reviving trade began to loosen both. Today you build the European arrangement as a system, then set it beside Song China, Dar al-Islam, Africa, the Americas, and South and Southeast Asia to say what that fragmentation cost and what it made possible.</p>
            </td>
        </tr>
        <tr>
            <td style="width: 20%; vertical-align: top; background-color: #f0f0f0;">
                <h3>LEARNING TARGETS</h3>
            </td>
            <td style="vertical-align: top;">
                <ol>
                    <li>I can explain how European political structures developed in the period c. 1200 to c. 1450.</li>
                    <li>I can describe how Christianity, feudalism, manorialism, and cities shaped European society.</li>
                    <li>I can explain how Europe compared with other regions of Unit 1 in state power, belief systems, and economic organization.</li>
                </ol>
            </td>
        </tr>
        <tr>
            <td style="width: 20%; vertical-align: top; background-color: #f0f0f0;">
                <h3>SUCCESS CRITERIA</h3>
            </td>
            <td style="vertical-align: top;">
                <ol>
                    <li>I can use evidence about monarchies, nobles, the Church, and decentralized power to explain European politics.</li>
                    <li>I can explain the roles of feudalism, manorialism, towns, guilds, and trade in European society.</li>
                    <li>I can compare Europe with Song China, Dar al-Islam, Africa, the Americas, or South and Southeast Asia.</li>
                </ol>
            </td>
        </tr>
        <tr>
            <td style="width: 20%; vertical-align: top; background-color: #f0f0f0;">
                <h3>BeHistorical Link</h3>
            </td>
            <td style="vertical-align: top;">
                <p><a class="inline_disabled" href="https://jeffandersonlogic.github.io/ap-world-history/unit-1/lesson-1-6-europe.html" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Topic 1.6 - Developments in Europe</a></p>
```

## APW - 1.7 - Comparison in the Period from c. 1200 to c. 1450

**Event title:** `APW - 1.7 - Comparison in the Period from c. 1200 to c. 1450`  
**Assignment to link:** `1.7 - Unit 1 Comparison`  
**Source data files:** `assets/data/lesson-1-7-comparison.js`, `assets/data/lesson-1-7-renderer-config.js`  
**Lesson page:** `unit-1/lesson-1-7-comparison.html`

```html
<table style="border-collapse: collapse; width: 100%; border-color: #000000; border-style: solid;" border="3" cellpadding="8">
    <tbody>
        <tr>
            <td style="width: 20%; vertical-align: top; background-color: #f0f0f0;">
                <h3>OVERVIEW</h3>
            </td>
            <td style="vertical-align: top;">
                <p>Comparison is a skill rather than a list, and today you practice it on everything Unit 1 has given you. You take two regions, name one meaningful similarity and one meaningful difference, and support each with specific evidence such as Song bureaucracy, Dar al-Islam scholarship, Mali trade, Inca roads, or European feudalism. Then you do the part most students skip: explain why that similarity or difference existed. A comparison that only names earns little; a comparison that explains is the essay.</p>
            </td>
        </tr>
        <tr>
            <td style="width: 20%; vertical-align: top; background-color: #f0f0f0;">
                <h3>LEARNING TARGETS</h3>
            </td>
            <td style="vertical-align: top;">
                <ol>
                    <li>I can compare methods of state building across regions from c. 1200 to c. 1450.</li>
                    <li>I can compare how belief systems shaped politics and society across Unit 1 regions.</li>
                    <li>I can write a clear AP-style comparison using specific evidence from at least two regions.</li>
                </ol>
            </td>
        </tr>
        <tr>
            <td style="width: 20%; vertical-align: top; background-color: #f0f0f0;">
                <h3>SUCCESS CRITERIA</h3>
            </td>
            <td style="vertical-align: top;">
                <ol>
                    <li>I can identify one meaningful similarity and one meaningful difference between two Unit 1 regions.</li>
                    <li>I can support each comparison with specific evidence such as Song bureaucracy, Dar al-Islam scholarship, Mali trade, Inca roads, or European feudalism.</li>
                    <li>I can explain why the similarity or difference existed instead of only naming it.</li>
                </ol>
            </td>
        </tr>
        <tr>
            <td style="width: 20%; vertical-align: top; background-color: #f0f0f0;">
                <h3>BeHistorical Link</h3>
            </td>
            <td style="vertical-align: top;">
```
